claims.text: High configurational entropy stabilizes the solid-solution structure of near-equiatomic multi-element nanoparticles at high service temperatures.
High configurational entropy suppresses elemental segregation in near-equiatomic nanoparticles.
High configurational entropy suppresses intermetallic phase formation at operating temperatures.
The initial near-equiatomic nanoparticles have a homogeneous, random distribution of constituent elements.
Skewing the composition away from equiatomic proportions while retaining the same element set lowers configurational entropy.
High mixing entropy produces a homogeneous elemental distribution in the nanoparticles.
High mixing entropy increases the energetic barrier for phase separation.
High mixing entropy increases the energetic barrier for intermetallic compound formation.
In equiatomic nanoparticles, entropy-mediated stabilization preserves a random solid-solution structure at elevated temperatures.
Reduced configurational entropy in non-equiatomic nanoparticles facilitates elemental segregation.
Reduced configurational entropy in non-equiatomic nanoparticles facilitates intermetallic-phase nucleation.
After identical high-temperature exposure, near-equiatomic nanoparticles will retain greater solid-solution phase stability and chemical homogeneity than non-equiatomic nanoparticles.
Non-equiatomic nanoparticles will exhibit phase segregation or emergent intermetallic phases under high-temperature exposure.
Segregation or intermetallic formation will be accompanied by changes in catalytic or thermoelectric properties.
The proposed entropy-stabilization mechanism is expected to hold in inert or mildly reactive environments.
Extreme oxidative or corrosive environments can compromise the predicted entropy-mediated stability.
Very small nanoparticle sizes can introduce kinetic or surface-energy effects that compromise the predicted behavior.
Kinetics, particle size, and surface chemistry can alter transition temperatures and the extent of phase separation.
